title: Word Search
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking visited cells with a separate grid versus marking them in place on the board with a sentinel character.

blocks.text: Given an m x n grid of characters board and a string word, return true if word exists in the grid. The word must be constructed from letters of SEQUENTIALLY ADJACENT cells (horizontally or vertically neighboring), and the same cell may not be used more than once within a single word.

blocks.caption: DFS with backtracking from every cell matching the word's first letter

blocks.text: Given a grid of letters and a target word, determine whether the word can be spelled out by moving between horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, never reusing a cell within the same attempt.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tracing a Word Through a Letter Maze With No Retracing
blocks.text: Like tracing a path through a grid of letter tiles with a pencil, spelling out a target word one letter at a time by moving to an adjacent tile at each step, never crossing back over a tile already used in the current trace. If a path leads to a dead end partway through, the pencil lifts back up to the last valid point and tries a different direction instead.

blocks.caption: A failed path unmarks its visited cell and lets a different direction be tried at that step

blocks.text: Before trying to find some clever formula, notice that this is fundamentally a search problem: try a direction, and if it fails, undo and try another, which is the defining shape of backtracking.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Any cell matching the word's FIRST letter is a valid place to start attempting a path.

Observation 2: From a matching cell, the next letter must be found in one of its 4 adjacent cells (up, down, left, right); if none match, this entire path attempt fails immediately.

Observation 3: A cell already used earlier in the CURRENT path attempt cannot be reused, so it must be marked as "in use" for the duration of exploring further from it, and un-marked the moment that exploration proves unsuccessful (backtracking).

Observation 4: If any explored direction from a given cell succeeds in completing the rest of the word, the search stops immediately and reports success; if all 4 directions fail, this cell's attempt fails, its mark is undone, and the search backs up to try a different choice made earlier.

Recognizing this "try, mark, recurse, unmark-if-failed" shape as classic depth-first search with backtracking is the key structural insight for this entire problem.

This is a classic DFS with backtracking pattern: explore a path fully before abandoning it, and always undo any temporary state changes (marking a cell as visited) the moment a path is found not to work.
Use a separate boolean grid to track which cells are currently part of the in-progress path, alongside the DFS and backtracking logic.

items: For every cell in the grid matching the word's first letter, start a depth-first search attempt.

At each step, check whether the current cell matches the needed letter and hasn't been visited yet in this attempt; if so, mark it visited, recursively try all 4 directions for the next letter, and unmark it if none succeed.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A separate visited grid tracks which cells are part of the current path attempt, keeping the original board completely untouched.
The DFS returns true immediately once k reaches the word's length, meaning every letter has been successfully matched.
visited[i][j] is reset to false immediately after all 4 directions have been tried, correctly implementing the backtracking undo step.

blocks.text: Every possible starting cell and every possible path from it is explored via DFS, so the correct answer is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols * 4^L) in the worst case, where L is the word's length, since each of the roughly rows*cols starting cells can branch into up to 4 directions at each of L steps.
Space: O(rows * cols) for the separate visited grid, plus O(L) for the recursion stack.

Limitation: maintaining a separate visited grid uses extra space, when the board itself can be temporarily modified in place (and restored afterward) to track the same information without any additional storage.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force uses a separate visited grid. Instead, temporarily overwrite the current cell's character directly in board with a sentinel value (one that can never match any letter, such as '#'), marking it as "in use" without any extra grid. After exploring all 4 directions, restore the original character before returning, whether the exploration succeeded or failed, correctly implementing backtracking using the board itself as the only storage needed.

Same DFS structure as the brute force, but instead of a separate visited array, save the current cell's character into a temporary variable, overwrite it with a sentinel character (like '#'), explore all 4 directions, then restore the saved character before returning from this recursive call.
Use the board itself as in-place visited-tracking, temporarily overwriting and restoring each cell as the search proceeds.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: A complete path (1,3) -> (2,3) -> (2,2) spells out "SEE" exactly, so the answer is true.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols * 4^L), the same asymptotic bound as the brute force, since the exploration pattern is unchanged.
Space: O(L) for the recursion stack alone, since no separate visited grid is needed.

Temporarily overwriting board[i][j] with a sentinel character (guaranteed never to match any letter of word) achieves exactly the same effect as a separate visited flag: any attempt to revisit this cell during the current exploration will immediately fail the character-match check. Restoring the original character before returning from the recursive call ensures that OTHER paths (explored later, from different starting points or different branches) still see the board in its true, original state.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Current cell matches the needed letter and is not the sentinel","Temporarily mark it, explore all 4 directions recursively"],["All 4 directions fail to complete the word","Restore the original character (undo the mark) before returning false, allowing other branches to reuse this cell"],["k reaches word.length","Every letter has been matched in sequence; return true immediately, propagating success up the call stack"]]}

items: The base case (k == word.length()) is checked FIRST, before any bounds or character checks, since success should be reported the instant the full word is matched.
The sentinel character '#' is chosen specifically because it can never appear in word (which consists only of English letters), guaranteeing it never accidentally matches.
Restoring board[i][j] = temp happens unconditionally after the 4 recursive calls, regardless of whether found ended up true or false, correctly cleaning up for both outcomes.

blocks.text: DFS with backtracking is defined by its "try, mark, recurse, unmark-if-failed" rhythm; here, the marking can be done directly on the input data itself (using a sentinel value) rather than via separate tracking storage, saving space without changing the algorithm's fundamental correctness or time complexity.

items: Forgetting to restore the original character after exploring all directions, which would permanently corrupt the board for other starting points or later exploration branches.
Checking the base case (k == word.length()) AFTER the bounds/character checks instead of before, which can cause an off-by-one error missing the exact moment of success.
Using a sentinel character that could actually appear in word, which would incorrectly allow a "visited" cell to still match during exploration.

items: Explicitly describe the backtracking rhythm ("mark, recurse, unmark") and justify why marking directly on the board (via a sentinel) avoids extra space, since this space-optimization detail is a common and expected follow-up in this specific problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find a path spelling out a target sequence using non-repeating adjacent grid cells" points toward DFS with backtracking, exploring each direction fully and undoing any temporary visited-marking the moment a path fails.

items: How would you optimize further for many repeated searches on the same board? Precomputing a set or trie of achievable words (via a single combined DFS pass building all reachable strings) can amortize the cost across many different target words.
How would this change if diagonal adjacency were also allowed? Simply add the 4 diagonal direction checks alongside the existing 4 orthogonal ones in the recursive exploration step.

What is the worst-case scenario for this algorithm's exponential time bound? A board filled entirely with the same repeated letter that also matches every letter of word, maximizing the branching factor at every single step of the search.

The foundational DFS-with-backtracking-on-a-grid pattern, closely related to other grid traversal and path-finding problems elsewhere in this category (e.g., Shortest Path in Binary Matrix uses BFS instead, since it needs the SHORTEST path rather than just existence).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(rows * cols * 4^L) time, O(rows * cols) + O(L) space.
Optimized (in-place sentinel marking): O(rows * cols * 4^L) time, O(L) space.

items: Pattern: DFS with backtracking, marking visited cells directly on the board using a sentinel character
Core Idea: Try a direction fully; if it fails, undo the temporary mark and try a different one, the classic backtracking rhythm
Time: O(rows * cols * 4^L)
Space: O(L) for the recursion stack (in-place marking avoids a separate visited grid)
Most Important Observation: Marking a cell as "in use" can be done directly on the input board via a sentinel value, avoiding the need for separate visited-tracking storage
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Mark with a sentinel, explore 4 directions recursively, restore on failure
